glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 22 places rich and poor alike under the LORD who made them, prizing a good name above riches and forbidding the exploitation of the weak, and at 22:17 it opens the words of the wise, given so that the son’s trust may be in the LORD.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Verses 1–16 close the collection headed “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1). At 22:17 a new call to hear “the words of the wise” begins longer instructions addressed personally to the son.

glance.label: Chapter Outline
glance.html:

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “The rich and the poor have this in common, The LORD is the maker of them all.” (Proverbs 22:2)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 22 opens by weighing two kinds of wealth. “A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches” (22:1), for the trust a man earns outlasts what he owns. Then every purse is set beside its owner’s Maker: “The rich and the poor have this in common, The LORD is the maker of them all” (22:2). The pair returns when “The rich rules over the poor” (22:7), and again with the man who squeezes the poor or courts the rich and “will surely come to poverty” (22:16).

Within those sayings stands the child. He is to be trained “in the way he should go” (22:6), God’s way, and the foolishness “bound up in the heart of a child” needs loving correction (22:15). Verse 6 describes how early formation usually bears fruit; it is no guarantee and never a verdict against parents whose children stray.

At verse 17 a teacher calls the son to “hear the words of the wise” and states his purpose: “So that your trust may be in the LORD” (22:19). Wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, begins in leaning on Him. The first instruction returns to the poor, and now the LORD enters the courtroom: “the LORD will plead their cause” (22:23). The Maker of rich and poor is the advocate of the weakest.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 22:1–5 — A Good Name and the Maker of All

A good name built on character outweighs great riches, and because the LORD made both rich and poor, every person stands before Him with the same dignity. The prudent see trouble coming and hide while the simple walk on into it, thorns and snares line the way of the perverse, and humility with the fear of the LORD leads to riches, honor, and life as a pattern of God’s goodness, not a formula for wealth.

Proverbs 22:6–16 — Training a Child and Justice for the Poor

A child trained in God’s way and corrected with love appears among sayings about the borrower’s bondage, the generous eye, and the oppressor whose rod of anger will fail. The scoffer must be driven out before strife will cease, the lazy man pleads an imaginary lion to stay home, the immoral woman’s mouth is a pit for the man the LORD abhors, and the section closes as it began, with the rich and the poor (22:7, 16).

Proverbs 22:17–21 — The Words of the Wise

A teacher calls the son to bend his ear, keep these sayings within him, and have them ready on his lips, so that his trust may be in the LORD. He has written excellent counsel so that the son may know what is certainly true and bring back a true answer to those who send him.

Proverbs 22:22–29 — Do Not Rob the Poor or Move the Landmark

The first warnings of the new collection forbid robbing the poor or crushing the afflicted at the gate, where cases were judged, because the LORD Himself will take up their cause against those who plunder them. The son must also keep away from the angry man whose ways he would learn, refuse pledges that could cost him his bed, and leave the ancient landmark where his fathers set it, while the man who excels in his work will stand before kings.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 22 puts money in its place. A good name is worth more than riches (22:1), and debt and surety are real forms of bondage that can take the bed from under a man (22:7, 27). That counsel calls for caution without forbidding every loan, and the riches tied to humility in 22:4 describe God’s general goodness to the humble, not a guarantee of wealth.

The chapter also shows how seriously God takes the poor. They share the same Maker as the rich (22:2), and He takes up their case against those who rob them (22:23), so cheating the weak sets a man against God Himself. For parents, 22:6 is a charge to train faithfully, not a promise that makes them answerable for every choice a grown child makes.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Rich and poor before their Maker. The LORD made them both, the generous share with the poor, and those who rob the poor will meet Him as their defender (22:2, 7, 9, 16, 22–23).

A good name. Character and gracious speech are worth more than silver and gold and win the friendship even of a king (22:1, 11).

Training and correction. A child is trained in the way he should go, and loving correction drives out the folly bound up in his heart (22:6, 15).

Trust in the LORD. The LORD’s eyes preserve knowledge, and the words of the wise are written so that the son’s trust may rest in Him (22:12, 19).

Snares for the soul. Thorns and snares lie in the way of the perverse (22:5), and friendship with an angry man can “set a snare for your soul” (22:24–25).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
A good name (22:1). A reputation built on character, so that others can trust what a person says and does. Its partner line, “Loving favor,” means being well thought of, and both are worth more than silver and gold.

Train up a child (22:6). To prepare a child from his earliest years for the life ahead. The phrase “in the way he should go” is debated; it most likely means the way of God, though some read it as the way that fits the child’s own nature. The saying is a principle of formation, not a guarantee.

The words of the wise (22:17). The opening of a new collection of longer instructions to the son. Its “excellent things” (22:20) translate a difficult word that some read as thirty, referring to thirty sayings; either way, the teacher points to the worth of what he has written.

Surety (22:26). Pledging oneself, by a handshake, to pay another person’s debt. The words of the wise repeat the warning of 6:1–5, for a pledge a man cannot pay may cost him his own bed (22:27).

The ancient landmark (22:28). A boundary stone marking a family’s land. Moving it quietly stole a neighbor’s inheritance, which the law of Moses also forbade (Deuteronomy 19:14).

focus: Proverbs 22 closes Solomon’s second group of sayings with a good name, training, generosity, and justice for the poor, and at 22:17 opens the words of the wise with a call to hear and trust the LORD and the first warnings that follow.

sections.title: A Good Name and the Maker of All
sections.summary: A good name is better than great riches, and the LORD is the Maker of rich and poor alike. The prudent foresee evil, and humility and the fear of the LORD bring riches, honor, and life.

sections.title: Training a Child and Justice for the Poor
sections.summary: A child is to be trained in the way he should go, and the borrower is servant to the lender. The generous are blessed, the scoffer is to be cast out, the lazy man makes excuses, and whoever oppresses the poor to gain riches will come to poverty.

sections.title: The Words of the Wise
sections.summary: The son is called to incline his ear to the words of the wise so that his trust may be in the LORD, and to learn the certainty of the words of truth.

sections.title: Do Not Rob the Poor or Move the Landmark
sections.summary: He must not rob the poor, for the LORD will plead their cause, nor befriend an angry man, become surety for debts, or remove the ancient landmark. The man who excels in his work will stand before kings.

1.brief: A good name, a reputation built on character, is worth choosing over great riches, and being well thought of is better than silver and gold. What people can trust in a person outlasts and outweighs anything he owns.
1.explain:
“A good name is to be chosen rather than great riches,”

A “name” in Scripture is more than a label. It is a person’s reputation, what others know and say about his character. A “good name” belongs to someone whose word can be relied on and whose dealings are honest. The saying is a choice between two treasures, and it says this one is “to be chosen,” deliberately preferred, over “great riches.” Money can be lost in a day, and it cannot buy back trust once trust is gone. A good name is built slowly through faithful living, and it outlasts whatever a person owns.

“Loving favor rather than silver and gold.”

The second line restates the first. “Loving favor” is the goodwill and esteem of others, being well thought of because of how one lives. It is worth more than “silver and gold,” the most precious metals of the ancient world. The verse does not despise money. It sets money in its place beneath character. Proverbs repeatedly warns that wealth gained by deceit or oppression destroys the very things this verse values, and the chapter will return to rich and poor in the very next saying, 22:2.
1.notes:
The Hebrew of the first line says simply “name”; the NKJV, with most English versions, adds “good” to bring out the sense. The KJV prints the supplied word in italics.

Ecclesiastes uses the same comparison: “A good name is better than precious ointment” (Ecclesiastes 7:1).

2.brief: Rich and poor share one thing in common: the LORD made them all. Every person, whatever his wealth, stands before God as His creature with equal dignity, and that truth calls the rich to treat the poor with respect.
2.explain:
“The rich and the poor have this in common,”

The rich and the poor seem to have little in common. They live in different houses, eat different food, and stand in very different places in society. Yet the verse says they share one thing, and it is the most important thing about them.

“The LORD is the maker of them all.”

Both were made by the LORD. Every person, whatever his wealth or poverty, is God’s creature, and that gives each one dignity before Him. The truth works in two directions. It humbles the rich, who owe their life to the same Maker as the poorest beggar, and it lifts the poor, who are not lesser people in God’s sight. Proverbs draws the practical conclusion elsewhere: “He who oppresses the poor reproaches his Maker” (14:31). This verse does not explain away inequality or approve the way the rich sometimes treat the poor. It grounds equal dignity and equal responsibility before God, and it prepares for the warnings about the poor that run through the rest of the chapter (22:7, 9, 16, 22–23).
2.notes: A similar saying appears in 29:13, “The poor man and the oppressor have this in common: The LORD gives light to the eyes of both” (29:13).

3.brief: Seeing trouble coming, the prudent person takes cover, but the simple keep walking straight into it and pay the price. Wisdom includes foresight, and the uncommitted, careless person suffers for his lack of it.
3.explain:
“A prudent man foresees evil and hides himself,”

The “prudent” man has practical good sense. He looks ahead and “foresees evil,” meaning trouble or danger coming his way, whether a bad deal, a dangerous companion, or the consequences of a foolish course. Seeing it, he “hides himself,” taking cover or changing direction before the trouble arrives. Wisdom includes foresight. The prudent person does not wait to learn everything by painful experience.

“But the simple pass on and are punished.”

The “simple” are the uncommitted and easily led, people who have not set their hearts on wisdom. They “pass on,” walking straight ahead without looking, and they “are punished,” suffering the consequences they could have avoided. Their problem is carelessness more than malice. They never stop to think where the road leads. The book’s opening lines promise “To give prudence to the simple” (1:4), and this saying shows why they need it.
3.notes: The saying appears again, almost word for word, in 27:12.

4.brief: Humility and the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, bring riches, honor, and life. These blessings flow from a life bowed before God, as a general pattern of His goodness and not a formula for wealth.
4.explain:
“By humility and the fear of the LORD”

Two qualities belong together here. “Humility” is a lowly view of oneself, the opposite of the pride Proverbs condemns. “The fear of the LORD” is a right view of God, seeing Him in His holiness and greatness and responding with awe, trust, and obedience. The two are closely linked. A person who sees God rightly cannot think too highly of himself, and humility is the soil in which reverence for God grows.

“Are riches and honor and life.”

From that root come “riches and honor and life.” These are the blessings God delights to give those who walk humbly before Him, and Proverbs speaks of them often. Like the book’s other sayings about wealth, this describes a general pattern of God’s goodness in His ordered world. It is not a formula that promises money to everyone who is humble. Many faithful people remain poor, and the book warns sharply against trusting riches, as in 23:4–5. “Riches” here is best understood as God’s blessing and provision broadly. The honor and life He gives last longer than any fortune.
4.notes: The first Hebrew word of the verse, which the NKJV renders “By,” is a noun meaning consequence or reward. Read that way, riches, honor, and life are what humility and the fear of the LORD lead to, and the ESV and the NASB (1995) render the verse with “reward.” The KJV margin offers the same reading.

5.brief: Thorns and traps line the path of the crooked, but the one who guards his life keeps far away from them. The perverse walk into needless pain, while careful living avoids it.
5.explain:
“Thorns and snares are in the way of the perverse;”

The “perverse” are the crooked, those whose lives twist away from what is right. Their path is lined with “thorns and snares,” painful obstacles and hidden traps. Thorns scratch and slow the traveler; snares catch him without warning. The crooked person’s way is full of needless pain because he keeps choosing paths that lead into it.

“He who guards his soul will be far from them.”

The contrast is the person who “guards his soul,” watching over his own life with care. He “will be far from them,” keeping his distance from the crooked road and its traps. This is the same practical wisdom as 22:3: seeing danger ahead and avoiding it. The guarding is active. A person protects his life by choosing his path carefully, by refusing crooked ways, and by staying out of places where snares are set.

6.brief: Parents are to train a child in the way he should go, God’s way, so that when he is old he will not turn from it. The saying describes how early formation usually bears fruit for a lifetime; it is a principle to live by, not a guarantee, and never a verdict against parents whose children stray.
6.explain:
“Train up a child”

To “train up” a child is to prepare him from his earliest years for the life ahead. The Hebrew verb behind “train up” is the one used elsewhere for dedicating a new house or the temple, so it carries the sense of starting something on its intended course. Training includes teaching, example, correction, and patient practice over many years. The “child” may be anyone from an infant to a young man, so the work begins early and continues through growing up.

“in the way he should go,”

The phrase “the way he should go” has been understood in two ways. The preferred reading takes it as God’s way, the path of wisdom and righteousness that Proverbs describes throughout. Parents are to set their child on that road. Another reading takes it as the way suited to the child’s own nature and calling, training that fits who he is. There is truth in that second idea, since wise parents pay attention to each child, but the book’s constant concern with “the way” of wisdom favors the first.

“And when he is old he will not depart from it.”

The second line describes the fruit of such training. Early formation usually lasts a lifetime. Habits, convictions, and loves learned in childhood tend to stay. This is a general principle, not a guarantee. Children grow into adults who make their own choices, and some who were trained well still wander. The verse must never be used to condemn parents whose grown children have strayed, and it gives no ground for treating a child’s choices as merely the parents’ doing. What it gives parents is a charge to train faithfully and the hope that such training usually bears fruit.
6.notes:
Apart from this verse, the Hebrew verb behind “train up” is used only of dedicating a new house in Deuteronomy 20:5 and the temple in 1 Kings 8:63 and 2 Chronicles 7:5. In those passages it marks the beginning of a building’s intended use, and that background fits the sense of starting a child on his course.

The Hebrew wording behind “in the way he should go” is shorter than the English, literally in his way, as the KJV margin notes. The Hebrew does not say whose standard defines “his way,” and that is the reason for the two readings of the line.

The KJV margin also offers “Catechise” as an alternative to “Train,” reflecting the older understanding of training as instruction.

7.brief: The rich rule over the poor, and the borrower becomes the servant of the lender. Debt places a person under another’s control, and this plain observation counsels caution about borrowing without forbidding it altogether.
7.explain:
“The rich rules over the poor,”

The first line states a plain fact of life in Solomon’s world and in ours. Those with money have power over those without it. The verse does not say this is how things ought to be. It describes how they are, and Proverbs elsewhere warns the rich not to abuse that power (22:16, 22–23).

“And the borrower is servant to the lender.”

The second line explains one way the rich come to rule. Debt places a person under another’s control. The borrower becomes the servant of the lender, bound by obligations he cannot easily escape. In the ancient world that could become literal servitude, when a debtor who could not pay was forced into service or could lose his children to the creditor as slaves (2 Kings 4:1). The saying is practical wisdom. It counsels caution about debt, especially for things a person does not need, and it encourages paying what is owed. It does not forbid all borrowing, and the law of Moses itself regulated lending to the poor. The chapter returns to the danger of debt in its warning against surety (22:26–27).

8.brief: Whoever sows wrongdoing will reap trouble, and the rod he used in anger against others will fail. The oppressor’s power to strike will come to an end, and the harvest of his injustice will be his own sorrow.
8.explain:
“He who sows iniquity will reap sorrow,”

The picture comes from farming. What a person plants determines what he harvests. The one who “sows iniquity,” planting injustice and wrongdoing in his dealings with others, “will reap sorrow,” trouble and grief. He may expect a profit, but the crop that comes up is misery. Scripture states the principle in many places, and Paul puts it simply: “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians 6:7).

“And the rod of his anger will fail.”

The “rod of his anger” is the power the unjust man uses to strike others, his means of oppressing and punishing those beneath him. That rod “will fail,” coming to an end. His power to harm does not last. In a section about rich and poor, the verse warns the oppressor that his ability to beat down the weak is temporary, and it comforts the oppressed that the tyrant’s rod will break.
8.notes:
The second line is difficult, and translations vary. The NKJV, ESV, and KJV say the rod “will fail,” and the NASB (1995) that it “will perish.” The KJV margin offers a different construction, that he will be consumed with the rod of his anger.

The ancient Greek translation (the Septuagint) adds a line after this verse saying that God blesses a cheerful and generous man. Paul’s words in 2 Corinthians 9:7, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7), closely resemble that added line and may echo it. The added line is not part of the Hebrew text that the NKJV translates.

9.brief: The person with a generous eye will be blessed, because he shares his bread with the poor. A heart that looks for ways to give receives blessing from the God who cares for the needy.
9.explain:
“He who has a generous eye will be blessed,”

In Hebrew, “a generous eye” is literally a good eye. The eye shows what the heart is looking for, and this person looks for ways to help. He notices need and responds to it. Such a person “will be blessed.” The verse does not say how, but Proverbs consistently teaches that God takes notice of generosity toward the poor and does not forget it.

“For he gives of his bread to the poor.”

The second line gives the reason and the evidence. He “gives of his bread,” sharing from his own food, the most basic provision. Bread here is not a symbol for something vague. It is daily food, and he shares it with “the poor” who lack it. Generosity in Proverbs is concrete. It costs something and meets a real need. Set beside 22:7 and 22:16, the verse shows another way to use wealth: the rich can rule over the poor, oppress them, or share with them, and only the last brings blessing.
9.notes: The opposite Hebrew expression, a bad or evil eye, describes a stingy, grasping person in 23:6 and 28:22, where the NKJV translates it “miser” and “evil eye.” The pair shows that in Proverbs the eye stands for a person’s attitude toward what he has and toward others’ needs.

10.brief: Drive out the scoffer, and quarreling goes with him; strife and insults come to an end. Sometimes peace requires removing the person who keeps stirring up contempt and conflict.
10.explain:
“Cast out the scoffer, and contention will leave;”

The scoffer is the proud mocker who will not accept correction and who stirs up trouble wherever he goes. When he cannot be taught, the verse gives a hard but necessary counsel: “Cast out the scoffer.” Remove him from the group, the household, or the assembly. When he goes, “contention will leave” with him. The quarreling followed him in, and it follows him out.

“Yes, strife and reproach will cease.”

The second line strengthens the first. “Strife,” the ongoing conflict, and “reproach,” the insults and shame that the scoffer’s contempt produces, “will cease.” Some troublemakers cannot be reasoned with, and peace in a community sometimes requires removing a person who keeps stirring up contempt and conflict. The verse does not encourage quick expulsion of anyone who disagrees. It speaks of the scoffer, the person who has already shown that he will not be corrected, as 9:7–8 describes. Patient correction comes first, but there comes a point when protecting the peace of the many is right.

11.brief: Whoever loves purity of heart and speaks with grace will have the king as his friend. Inner integrity joined to kind speech earns trust even in the highest places.
11.explain:
“He who loves purity of heart”

The first quality is inward. This person “loves purity of heart.” He does not merely avoid obvious sin; he values a clean heart, sincere motives, and integrity that runs all the way through.

“And has grace on his lips,”

The second quality is outward. He “has grace on his lips,” speaking with kindness, wisdom, and courtesy. His words are pleasant and fitting. Inner purity and gracious speech belong together, because the mouth speaks from what fills the heart.

“The king will be his friend.”

The result is favor in high places. “The king will be his friend.” A wise ruler values people he can trust and whose words are both honest and gracious. Such people are rare in a royal court, where flattery and scheming are common. The saying describes the honor integrity often brings. As elsewhere in Proverbs, it states what is generally true, and it also shows what kind of person a good king should want near him.
11.notes: The Hebrew of this verse is compact, and the KJV construes it differently: that the king is his friend because of the grace of his lips. The KJV margin gives the reading the NKJV follows.

12.brief: Knowledge is kept safe under the LORD’s watchful eyes, but He overturns the words of the faithless. Truth is under God’s protection, while the speech of the treacherous will not stand.
12.explain:
“The eyes of the LORD preserve knowledge,”

The “eyes of the LORD” picture His watchful attention over all things. Those eyes “preserve knowledge,” keeping true knowledge safe and guarding the people who hold it. Truth is under God’s protection. Whatever people may do to suppress or distort it, the LORD watches over what is true, and in the end it will stand.

“But He overthrows the words of the faithless.”

The contrast is the “faithless,” the treacherous people who break trust and twist the truth. God “overthrows” their words, frustrating their lies and schemes so that they do not stand. Their clever speech may succeed for a while, but it will not last. The verse fits the chapter’s concern with the poor and the powerful. Those who use deceit to gain an advantage over others will find that God Himself works against their words.

13.brief: Afraid of nothing but work, the lazy man insists there is a lion outside and that he will be killed in the streets. The absurd excuse exposes his habit of inventing dangers so he can stay at home, a mark of the lazy man throughout Proverbs.
13.explain:
“The lazy man says, ‘There is a lion outside!’”

The lazy man always has an excuse, and this one is absurd. He claims, “There is a lion outside!” He is not really afraid of a lion. He is afraid of work, and he invents a danger so he can stay home.

“I shall be slain in the streets!”

He adds drama to the excuse: “I shall be slain in the streets!” The exaggeration exposes him. The lazy man’s imagination is very active when it comes to reasons not to do what needs doing. Proverbs paints him the same way in 26:13, where he says, “There is a lion in the road!” (26:13). Laziness hides behind excuses that sound like caution. The verse is not about genuine danger or legitimate fear. It describes the habit of inventing obstacles to avoid responsibility, a habit Proverbs treats as both foolish and harmful.

14.brief: An immoral woman’s mouth is a deep pit, and the one under the LORD’s displeasure falls into it. Her seductive words are a trap, and the man who has already turned from God is the one who tumbles in (compare 7:21–23).
14.explain:
“The mouth of an immoral woman is a deep pit;”

The “immoral woman” is the adulteress of the book’s opening chapters, an outsider to the young man’s home and to God’s ways. Her “mouth” is her seductive speech: flattery, enticement, and promises of pleasure. That mouth “is a deep pit,” like the pits dug to trap animals, easy to fall into and almost impossible to climb out of. Chapter 7 showed her words at work: “With her enticing speech she caused him to yield” (7:21). The danger begins with listening.

“He who is abhorred by the LORD will fall there.”

The second line is sobering. The one who falls into the pit is “abhorred by the LORD,” a man under His displeasure. The line does not mean that God pushes an innocent man in. The man who has already turned his back on God, rejecting His word and His ways, has no protection against her words. His fall is both the result of turning from God and a judgment on it. The man who fears the LORD and keeps His word has a guard against the snare, as the father taught in chapters 5–7.
14.notes:
Proverbs uses the same image in 23:27, “For a harlot is a deep pit, And a seductress is a narrow well” (23:27).

The Hebrew word behind “immoral woman” is plural here, literally strange women, which the KJV (“strange women”) and ESV (“forbidden women”) reflect. The NKJV and the NASB (1995) render it as singular, treating the plural as a description of a type of woman.

15.brief: Foolishness is tied tight in the heart of a child, but the rod of correction will drive it far away. Children need loving, consistent correction because folly comes naturally to them; the verse never justifies harshness, rage, or abuse.
15.explain:
“Foolishness is bound up in the heart of a child;”

Proverbs does not picture children as naturally wise. “Foolishness,” the moral folly that resists instruction and goes its own way, “is bound up in the heart of a child.” It is tied tight, knotted in, part of him from the start. Children do not need lessons in selfishness or defiance. That is why training and correction are needed, as 22:6 has already said. A child left to himself will not grow into wisdom on his own, as the book says elsewhere: “a child left to himself brings shame to his mother” (29:15).

“The rod of correction will drive it far from him.”

The “rod of correction” is the tool of discipline in its biblical setting, and the verse says it “will drive” foolishness “far from him.” The rod includes physical correction, yet the discipline Proverbs speaks of is broader than punishment. It is the whole work of teaching, guiding, correcting, and training a child toward maturity, and it reflects the way the LORD corrects the son in whom He delights, as 3:11–12 describes. As at 13:24, correction aims at restoration, turning a child from a harmful course toward what is right. It is calm, consistent, and given with love. It is never an outlet for a parent’s anger or frustration, and it never justifies harshness, rage, or abuse. The goal is a child set free from the folly that would harm him, one who has learned the right way and not merely learned to fear punishment.
15.notes: Proverbs speaks of the rod in the correction of children at 13:24, 22:15, 23:13–14, and 29:15. The fuller discussion of discipline belongs to 13:24, and each later saying adds its own emphasis. Here the stress falls on the folly already present in a child’s heart.

16.brief: Whoever oppresses the poor to build his wealth, or gives gifts to the rich to win favor, will surely come to poverty himself. Whether he squeezes the weak or flatters the strong, the man who chases riches in these ways ends up with less, closing Solomon’s collection on the theme of rich and poor.
16.explain:
“He who oppresses the poor to increase his riches,”

The first figure squeezes the weak to make himself richer. He “oppresses the poor,” taking advantage of people who cannot fight back, through unfair wages, crushing interest, or seizure of their goods, all “to increase his riches.”

“And he who gives to the rich,”

The second figure flatters the strong. He “gives to the rich,” offering gifts to powerful people to win favor or gain an advantage. One exploits those beneath him, and the other courts those above him. Both are using people to get ahead.

“will surely come to poverty.”

Both “will surely come to poverty.” The man who chases riches in these ways ends up with less. Oppressing the poor sets him against God, who defends them in 22:22–23, and gifts to the rich are often wasted on people who need nothing and give nothing back. The saying closes Solomon’s long collection on the theme of rich and poor that opened this chapter at 22:2 and returned at 22:7. Like other sayings about money, it states a general pattern and sets no timetable, but it warns that wealth gained by using people does not last.
16.notes:
The Hebrew of this verse is compressed, and translations arrange it differently. The 1984 NIV adds “both” to make clear that the two figures share one end.

With this saying the collection headed “The proverbs of Solomon” (10:1) comes to an end, and a new call to listen begins at 22:17.

17.brief: Here a new collection begins, as the teacher calls the son to bend his ear to the words of the wise and set his heart on what he teaches. The call to listen opens a set of longer instructions addressed personally to the learner.
17.explain:
“Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise,”

A new collection begins here. After hundreds of short sayings, a teacher speaks personally again, much as the father did in chapters 1–9. To “Incline your ear” is to lean in and listen closely. What the son is to hear are “the words of the wise,” sayings that come from wise teachers and are now gathered for him. The phrase introduces the instructions that run to 24:22, and the book promised at its start to help the reader understand “The words of the wise and their riddles” (1:6).

“And apply your heart to my knowledge;”

Hearing is not enough. The son must “apply” his “heart,” setting his whole inner self on what he is taught. The teacher calls it “my knowledge,” so the words of the wise reach the son through a teacher who has made them his own and hands them on personally. Wisdom is received through attentive ears and a willing heart. This call opens a set of longer instructions, many of them two or three verses long, addressed directly to the learner.
17.notes:
A second short collection is introduced later with “These things also belong to the wise” (24:23), which confirms that “the words of the wise” names a body of sayings.

The commands to hear and to set the heart, followed by reasons, resemble the father’s appeals in chapters 1–9 (compare 4:20–22).

18.brief: Keeping these sayings stored inside is a pleasant thing, and the teacher wants them ready on the son’s lips. Wisdom is meant to be held in the heart and then spoken, not merely heard once.
18.explain:
“For it is a pleasant thing if you keep them within you;”

The teacher gives a reason to listen. It is “a pleasant thing” to “keep them within you,” storing these sayings deep inside. Wisdom is useful, and it is also good to have. The words become part of the person, and there is a satisfaction in carrying truth within that the person who never learns does not know.

“Let them all be fixed upon your lips,”

What is stored within must also be ready to speak. “Fixed upon your lips” means established there and ready for use. The teacher wants wisdom to move from the heart to the mouth, so that when the moment comes for counsel, correction, or a true answer, the right words are at hand. This prepares for 22:21, where the son must “answer words of truth” to others. Wisdom is meant to be held in the heart and then spoken.
18.notes: In Hebrew, “within you” is literally in your belly, as the KJV margin notes. The belly here stands for the innermost part of a person, the place where the sayings are to be kept.

19.brief: His purpose is stated plainly: that the son’s trust may be in the LORD, and for that reason he has taught him today, even him. The aim of this wisdom is not cleverness but confident reliance on God, and the instruction is personal and urgent.
19.explain:
“So that your trust may be in the LORD;”

Here the teacher states the purpose of everything that follows: “So that your trust may be in the LORD.” The words of the wise are not given to make the son clever or successful for his own sake. They are given to lead him to rely on God. That is a striking aim for practical sayings about money, speech, food, and friendship. Every instruction in this collection, however ordinary its subject, is meant to bring the learner into confident dependence on the LORD. Wisdom, the skill of living life God’s way, begins and ends in trusting Him.

“I have instructed you today, even you.”

The instruction is personal and urgent. “Today” calls for attention now. “Even you” singles out the learner. The teacher is not addressing a crowd in general. He is speaking to this son, and through him to every reader who receives these words as spoken to himself.

20.brief: With a question, the teacher points to the excellent things of counsel and knowledge he has written for the son. The question underlines the worth of what follows, carefully set down for the learner’s good.
20.explain:
“Have I not written to you excellent things”

The teacher asks a question that expects the answer yes. He has “written” these things, so the instruction is careful, preserved teaching rather than a passing remark. He calls them “excellent things,” words of high value and noble quality. The question underlines their worth and calls the son to take them seriously.

“Of counsels and knowledge,”

The content is “counsels and knowledge,” advice for living and understanding of what is true. Counsel tells a person what to do, and knowledge helps him see why. Both are needed, and both are given here for the son’s good. The sentence runs on into 22:21, which states what these writings are meant to accomplish.
20.notes:
The word translated “excellent things” is one of the hardest in the chapter. The letters written in the Hebrew text spell a word that literally means three days ago, the day before yesterday, and it is used in expressions meaning formerly or previously. A note in the margin of Hebrew Bibles directs the reader to a different word, which the NKJV, the NASB (1995), and the KJV understand as excellent or noble things. The ancient Greek, Syriac, Aramaic, and Latin translations have three times instead, and the YLT also renders “three times.” Many modern scholars read the margin’s word with different vowels as thirty, and the ESV and NLT translate “thirty sayings.”

The “thirty” reading is tied to the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope, a wisdom text arranged in thirty chapters and preserved on a papyrus in the British Museum. E. A. Wallis Budge published the text in 1922 and 1923, and in 1924 Adolf Erman pointed out close parallels between it and the sayings that follow, especially 22:17–23:11, and proposed reading “thirty” here. Many scholars have discussed the parallels since. How the two are related, and in which direction any influence ran, is debated. Whatever their history, these sayings stand in Scripture under the purpose stated in 22:19.

21.brief: These sayings are written so the son may know the certainty of the words of truth and give true answers to those who send to him. Wisdom makes a person reliable, someone others can trust to bring back an accurate word.
21.explain:
“That I may make you know the certainty of the words of truth,”

The purpose clause explains why the excellent things were written. The teacher wants the son to “know the certainty of the words of truth,” to be sure of what is true and to rest on it. Truth here is reliable and solid, something a person can stand on. In a world full of rumor, flattery, and false witnesses, the son needs words he can be certain of.

“That you may answer words of truth”

Knowing the truth leads to speaking it. The son is to “answer words of truth,” giving accurate and reliable replies when he is asked. This takes up 22:18, where the sayings were to be “fixed upon your lips.” Wisdom makes a person dependable, someone whose answer can be trusted.

“To those who send to you?”

In the NKJV the son answers “those who send to you,” people who come to him or send messengers to him for counsel and information. A person who knows the truth becomes someone others can turn to with confidence. Whoever asks, the wise son can be relied on to give a true word to those who depend on him.
21.notes: Translations differ on the final phrase. The NKJV and KJV read it as people who send to the son. The KJV margin, the ESV, NASB, and NLT read it as those who sent him, picturing the son as a messenger who brings back an accurate report.

22.brief: Do not rob the poor because they are poor and easy to take from, and do not crush the afflicted in the city gate where cases are judged. The first warning of the new collection forbids taking advantage of those who cannot defend themselves.
22.explain:
“Do not rob the poor because he is poor,”

The first instruction of the new collection goes straight to the poor. “Because he is poor” names the robber’s motive. The poor man is easy to take from. He has no money for a defense, no powerful friends, and no way to strike back, so robbing him seems safe. The command forbids exploiting someone precisely because he is weak. That covers outright theft, and it also covers unfair wages, crushing interest, and any scheme that takes advantage of the defenseless.

“Nor oppress the afflicted at the gate;”

The “gate” of an Israelite city was where the elders sat and cases were judged. To “oppress the afflicted at the gate” is to crush the poor through the courts, by bribery, false testimony, or legal maneuvering. Injustice in the very place meant to provide justice is especially wicked. The “afflicted” are those already pressed down by poverty or trouble, and the command forbids pressing them further.

23.brief: Behind the command stands the LORD Himself, who will plead their cause and take the life of those who plunder them. The poor have a defender in court, and He is far stronger than any oppressor.
23.explain:
“For the LORD will plead their cause,”

The reason for the command is the LORD Himself. He “will plead their cause.” The language comes from the courtroom: God takes up the case of the poor as their advocate. The poor man who cannot afford a defender has one, and He is the Judge of all the earth. Whoever robs the poor will find himself facing God in court. The verse is more than a call to private charity. It declares that God stands with the weak against those who exploit them.

“And plunder the soul of those who plunder them.”

The second line describes the outcome. God will “plunder the soul,” taking the life, “of those who plunder them.” The punishment fits the crime. Those who stripped the poor of their goods will be stripped of their own lives. The repeated word “plunder” makes the point unmistakable: what the oppressor did to the poor, the LORD will do to him.
23.notes: The promise returns at 23:10–11 in the warning about the fields of the fatherless: “For their Redeemer is mighty; He will plead their cause against you” (23:11).

24.brief: Do not make friends with a hot-tempered man or keep company with someone given to rage. Companions influence character, and anger is contagious.
24.explain:
“Make no friendship with an angry man,”

In Hebrew, the “angry man” is literally a master of anger, someone ruled by his temper. The son is told not to make him a friend. The warning does not require avoiding everyone who has ever lost his temper. It concerns close companionship with a person whose life is marked by anger.

“And with a furious man do not go,”

The second line repeats the warning. A “furious man” is given to rage, and the son must not “go” with him, keeping his company or walking his road. In Proverbs the people we walk with influence how we walk: “He who walks with wise men will be wise” (13:20). Friendship is never neutral.

25.brief: Otherwise you will learn his ways and set a trap for your own soul. The danger is not only his outbursts but that his habits will become yours and lead you into ruin.
25.explain:
“Lest you learn his ways”

The reason for the warning is that anger spreads. Spend enough time with a hot-tempered person, and you “learn his ways.” His habits of reacting, blaming, and lashing out become yours, often without your noticing. People absorb the patterns of those closest to them, and a temper learned in friendship can be hard to unlearn.

“And set a snare for your soul.”

The result is a trap for one’s own life. The son who learns anger will “set a snare for your soul,” preparing his own ruin. The angry man’s outbursts are bad enough, yet the greater danger is that his ways will become the son’s. Anger damages relationships and leads to rash words and violent deeds, and once it becomes a habit it traps the one who carries it. Choosing companions wisely is one way of guarding one’s life, the same guarding commended in 22:5.

26.brief: Do not be among those who shake hands on a pledge or put up security for other people’s debts. The teacher repeats the book’s warning against rash surety (compare 6:1–5).
26.explain:
“Do not be one of those who shakes hands in a pledge,”

To shake hands in a pledge was the gesture that sealed an agreement to guarantee someone else’s debt. With a handshake a man bound himself to pay if the borrower did not. The teacher says plainly, “Do not be one of those” who do this. Proverbs has already warned the son at length about such pledges in 6:1–5.

“One of those who is surety for debts;”

The second line names the practice. A “surety” is a guarantor, someone who stands behind another person’s loan. Proverbs warns against this repeatedly because it puts a person at the mercy of someone else’s choices and ability to pay. This is practical wisdom about money. It does not forbid helping others. It counsels against promising what one cannot afford to lose. A person who wants to help is wiser to give what he is able and willing to give than to guarantee a debt he may not be able to pay.

27.brief: If you have nothing to pay with, why should the bed be taken out from under you? Cosigning can cost a person even the most basic necessities, which is why it should not be done lightly.
27.explain:
“If you have nothing with which to pay,”

The teacher presses the danger with a scenario. The borrower defaults, and the guarantor must pay, but he has “nothing with which to pay.” He promised more than he had.

“Why should he take away your bed from under you?”

Then the creditor comes to collect and takes “your bed from under you.” The bed stands for the most basic things a household needs, and even these could be taken to cover the debt. The picture is of losing even basic necessities because of a careless handshake. The question “Why should he...?” asks the son to think. Why put yourself in that position? A pledge made lightly can strip a family of what it needs to live, and the loss falls on the one who meant only to help.

28.brief: Do not move the ancient boundary stone that your fathers set in place. Shifting a landmark was a quiet way of stealing a neighbor’s land and inheritance, and the command protects what God gave each family (compare Deuteronomy 19:14).
28.explain:
“Do not remove the ancient landmark”

A “landmark” was a boundary stone marking the edge of a family’s land. In Israel the land was divided among the tribes and families as their inheritance from the LORD, and the boundary stones recorded those divisions. Moving one, even a short distance, quietly took land from a neighbor. Because the stones were “ancient,” set long ago, few people might remember exactly where they belonged, and a dishonest man could take advantage of that. The law of Moses forbade the practice: “You shall not remove your neighbor’s landmark, which the men of old have set” (Deuteronomy 19:14).

“Which your fathers have set.”

The boundary was set by “your fathers,” the earlier generations who received the land. To move it was to steal both property and inheritance, the portion God had given a family to pass down. That is why Naboth refused to sell his vineyard to the king: “The LORD forbid that I should give the inheritance of my fathers to you!” (1 Kings 21:3). The command protects the weak, whose land was most easily taken, and it honors God’s gift to each family. The warning returns in 23:10 with special concern for the fatherless.
28.notes: In Israel, moving a neighbor’s boundary stone fell under a public curse, pronounced before all the people: “Cursed is the one who moves his neighbor’s landmark” (Deuteronomy 27:17).

29.brief: Picture a man who excels at his work: he will stand before kings, not before obscure men. Skill and diligence open doors to honor and service in high places.
29.explain:
“Do you see a man who excels in his work?”

The teacher asks the son to look at someone. The man who “excels in his work” is skilled, quick, and capable at what he does. The Hebrew word behind “excels” means quick and skilled, and the same word describes Ezra as “a skilled scribe in the Law of Moses” (Ezra 7:6). Skill like that comes from diligence, practice, and care.

“He will stand before kings;”

Such a man “will stand before kings.” To stand before a king was to serve in his presence and be trusted with important work. Skill and faithfulness open doors to honor. Joseph is an example. He “stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt” (Genesis 41:46) after God gave him wisdom and he proved faithful in every task.

“He will not stand before unknown men.”

He will not remain in the service of “unknown men,” people of no standing. His work will be noticed. The saying is a general observation about how excellence is usually recognized, not a promise that every skilled worker will rise to high office. It also shows that ordinary work done well matters, and that God can use it in high places.
29.notes: Where the NKJV has “unknown men,” the ESV and the NASB (1995) have “obscure men,” and the KJV has “mean” men, with a margin note that the Hebrew means “obscure men.”
